text: The physics in the last three lessons is shared across every trapped-ion system, but the two companies that have turned it into commercial hardware — IonQ and Quantinuum — have made different engineering choices about which ion to use and how to scale past a single chain.

IonQ builds its processors around trapped ytterbium ions, using the single-chain, laser-controlled architecture from this chapter: ions cooled toward their motional ground state, individually addressed with laser pulses, entangled via Mølmer-Sørensen-style gates through the chain's shared motional modes. IonQ has marketed the all-to-all connectivity within its chains as a central differentiator relative to nearest-neighbor superconducting hardware, and makes its systems available through major cloud platforms, letting developers submit circuits without owning the hardware directly.

Quantinuum, formed from the 2021 merger of Honeywell Quantum Solutions and Cambridge Quantum, builds its H-Series systems around ions like calcium and barium — often using one species as the qubit and a second as a sympathetic-cooling partner that can be re-cooled with lasers without disturbing the qubit ion's stored state. Quantinuum's systems use a QCCD architecture — quantum charge-coupled device — where a single chip-scale trap is divided into zones, some for storing idle ions, others for gates, with electrode voltages dynamically shuttling ions between them. That's the practical answer to motional-mode crowding: rather than growing one chain indefinitely, keep chains short and shuttle ions to let any ion eventually interact with any other.

Both companies, like every vendor in this course, publish qubit counts and fidelity figures that improve across hardware generations and get used heavily in marketing. As of recent years, both have reported qubit counts in the dozens and two-qubit gate fidelities often quoted at or above roughly 99 percent — but the exact figures depend on which system generation and which benchmark methodology is being cited. The durable, hardware-level facts worth keeping are architectural: which ion species, whether a QCCD design with shuttling is used, and why — not whichever press release happens to be current.
Next lesson: you now have two full architectures to compare. Superconducting qubits from Chapter 1, and trapped ions from this chapter, side by side — honestly, with neither one declared the winner.
